en: Set things right without being deceived.
The broad Keng-Kol plain and Suusamyr
Lie on the road Kongurbay once took;
It was the army that kept deceiving
Our magnanimous father Manas.
Ever since Bedel, deception
Has been that swine’s way.
He was the son of a mighty sorcerer,
A man unlike other mortals,
A lion whose fame
Spread throughout the world.
My princely uncle, hear this from me;
Hear the cunning deed I mean to do!
I shall saddle Buurul properly.
Is any oath owed to that enemy?
I shall bow down like the Chinese.
When they seize their idol
And turn me against the foe,
Do not surge forward, uncle, thinking,
“The Chinese have broken and fled.”
Do not cast a turmoil no man could endure
Upon Külchoro alone.
Do not think, “He has gone
Into the midst of the stinking Manchus,
And worships as his god
The bronze idol
They fashioned with their own hands.”
Do not mourn my place in the ranks.
Do not rage and bristle,
My lionhearted uncle and sultan,
And make my misery boil over.
Among that Khagan’s forty khans,
I shall spill their blood and crush them
And stage a spectacle.
Understand what I have said:
To deceive and turn the Chinese,
My precious uncle, heed my words.
If you give me Buurul, I shall mount him
And move among them,
Making them call me khan, not slave.
The heirloom musket left by your father—
Now the enemy we must shoot has appeared.
If you give me Akkelte, I shall take it,
Sling it over my broad shoulder,
And then go to the Kalcha.
Making them say, ‘He surpasses his father Manas,’
I shall thus seize the hearts
Of Beijing and China’s forty tribes.
As though some great lord had arrived,
Let the Chinese swarm out and run;
As though they beheld my khan and father Manas.
Let the Khagan despair of life.
If you give me Akolpok, I shall put it on,
Make Buurul prance,
And ride among you.
If the Chinese do not deceive me,
I shall drive them all the way to Beijing itself.
I shall buckle the gray purse at my waist
And, looking like Khan Almambet himself—
If not himself, then his dark-eyed likeness—
I shall proudly ride Buurul
And enter their midst.
Upon the forty tribes of China and Beijing’s realm
I shall lay a terrible oppression.
Thus shall I avenge
The lions who passed into Judgment
And the heroes who died untimely deaths.
If you bind six pennons to its shaft—
Its haft stout and its point sharp—
Give me the patterned spear as a gift.
I shall accept the spear as a gift
And tread the road of hardship.
When he scowls and bristles—
The infidel son of Kaldai,
The warrior Khan Kongurbay—
I shall bring slaughter upon mighty Dyngshaa,
Massacre the Chinese,
And destroy this multitude.
I own no livestock to halt in the valley;
Against my own kinsman, the Kalcha,
I have no life to spare from death.
I own no herds to spread upon the river terrace;
Let the countless Chinese wage war—
I have no life to spare from battle.”
Then your prince spoke again
To the radiant Choro:
“For a son like you, who turns the foe,
Father—my dear Külchoro—
Let my Buurul be sacrificed!
For a son like you,
Let your uncle’s racehorse be sacrificed!”
Unable to say, “I will not give it,”
Or rebuff the valiant man’s desire,
Unable to say, “Leave it, boy,”
Or break the desperate hero’s heart,
He dismounted and gave him Buurul,
And unfastened and gave him his sash.
He readied all the war gear,
Strapped on the naked sword,
And placed it in mighty Külchoro’s hands.
He clothed him in armor no bullet could pierce,
Revealing him as a true lion.
Into the hands of the flashing Choro
He gave the equipment,
And sent the warrior on his way.
Do not ask what was done for the young man:
They had ninety black bull-calves
Slaughtered and sent forth.
Lest someone’s evil eye strike him,
They offered them as sacrifice for the Choro.
Külchoro asked his uncle
For the racehorse,
And sprang up without touching
The stirrups with golden soles.
Was he not gray-wolf born?
To the marsh of Üyrülmö,
To the summit of Teek-Too,
Went the true falcon, gray-wolf born—
Külchoro, the intercessor,
The swift-moving lion Choro,
The nimble, kinsman-warrior Choro,
Born after Almambet of old,
After your lord and champion,
That noble elder who subdued the world—
A lion Choro born in his wake.
The precious prince Semetey
Stood upon the ridge of Kök-Sengir,
Upon its overhanging spur.
The great host of Argyn and Kyrgyz
Stood gathered in a throng.
In the marsh of Chogulma,
Chinese and Kyrgyz seethed,
Swarming like black worms,
And held a common assembly.
They stood there gathered;
Külchoro moved between them,
The seasoned lion Choro,
A warrior who knew the ways
Of both Chinese and Kyrgyz.
The sight overwhelmed the mind:
Gray-wolf Semetey had encamped upon a ridge.
He looked like the blue mountain crag,
Like the cool shade
Of a cloud above the peaks,
Like the gaping throat
Of a sheer ravine.
The mountain crest seemed but a ridge beside him,
And he seemed as vast as half the valley;
He looked ready to devour whoever approached,
That broad and fearsome firebrand.
His bullets were like stones in a ravine,
And the smoke from his nostrils
Like ridges across the broad blue steppe;
Such was his awesome depth to behold.
When Semetey encamped there,
His boundless pavilion and court
Seemed spacious enough for all mankind to rest.
Twelve thousand men lay utterly still,
As though horses and all had vanished inside it.
From every side
It seemed they were playing ordo;
Such was the prince’s encampment.
Forty patterned silk carpets
Were spread ridge upon ridge.
The red banner inherited
From precious Khan Manas
Was raised sky-high.
It became a golden-crescent banner,
Amid clamorous battle cries;
It became a sun-tasseled standard,
Amid deep, resounding tumult.
Making the whole world rejoice,
They boiled barren young mares
In the great communal cauldrons.
The people descended in a mass;
Brave Semetey and Khan Bakai
Set about their preparations.
The golden-crescent patterned spear
Was lifted high into the heavens,
Beginning to make
The whole wide world bloom.
Leave that matter there;
Now begin the tidings of Kongurbay
And the forty tribes of China.
Their scout sent to reconnoiter,
Their envoy passing between the hosts,
Was a man of many guises.
Külchoro, son of Almambet,
Became the mediator,
And the gray-wolf lion moved between them.
The infidel son of Kaldai,
The warrior Khan Kongurbay,
Ezkara and their khans—
The time had come when he deceived them,
While the fortunate Choro went between the hosts
And drew alongside them.
He came before Kongurbay,
And began delivering
The weighty speech the hero intended.
His knee bent to the earth,
And the blazing firebrand
Did homage to the Kalcha,
Bowing like a bride.
As the Choro stood thus,
The bearded Kalcha elders,
The elders headed by Ezkara,
Their khans worshipped stones,
Their people thronged in multitudes,
And made Choro their very heart.
Everyone who went over, he won to his side,
And among the forty tribes of China
He became a formidable power:
“He has been living among the Burut,
Yet Choro knew well
That Burkan is God.
To call him a Burut Kyrgyz
Is idle slander.
He declares Burkan to be God;
His faith is loftier than ours.
He is a champion and a lion,
A hero beyond all measure,
A warrior fit to guard
This Beijing of the Khakan.
By cruel fate he was born
And lived among the Burut,
Yet he knew our god Burkan
Better than we ourselves.
Unable to learn the truth of Burkan,
He barely endured among the Burut.
Now he has returned and found his kin,
And this accursed boy has recognized
That Burkan is divine.
He is the true descendant
Of khans who gird the royal belt.
Of the khans who wear fine robes,
He is the mightiest himself;
He is the watchful dark eye
Of the kaldai in the karapchy coat;
Among the Manchu in coats of mail,
He is the very champion.
He is the offspring of true China,
The mainstay of Chin-Machin.
Without wearing out the racers
Of these forty tribes of China,
Without burdening their hearts—
He is a man fit to defend it.
For a khan’s descendant to wander homeless
Is, as we see, a grievous, senseless thing.
With cotton sash and broad boots,
Kongurbai, khan of the shaven-headed monks,
Stands one spear-cast above the rest;
His fortune is complete.
The powerful Chinese, the realm of forty khans,
Have a son fit to defend them.
He is both a strongman and a giant,
And master of our Great Beijing.
